summary.text: If primes \(p,q\) have different final digits, satisfy \(pq\le150\), and neither divides \(d\), then \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\), so some \(0\le i<pq\) makes \(a+id\) divisible by both primes and hence inadmissible. A finite divisibility analysis using \(2,3,5,7,11,13,17\) shows that every \(d\le2025\) leaves such a pair uncovered, since all alternative covering patterns would force a product greater than \(2025\) to divide \(d\).

full_proof.text:
Let a positive integer be called lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same final decimal digit. We prove that there do not exist integers
\[
a\ge 2,\qquad 1\le d\le 2025
\]
such that all 150 numbers
\[
a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
are lopsided.

We first establish the basic obstruction that will be used throughout.

**Obstruction lemma.** Let \(p\) and \(q\) be primes whose final decimal digits are different. Suppose
\[
pq\le 150,
\]
and suppose that neither \(p\) nor \(q\) divides \(d\). Then among the 150 terms \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\), there is a term that is not lopsided.

Indeed, because \(p\) and \(q\) have different final digits, they are distinct primes. Since neither divides \(d\), we have
\[
\gcd(d,p)=\gcd(d,q)=1,
\]
and hence
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Thus \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\). Choose an integer \(i\) satisfying
\[
i\equiv -a d^{-1}\pmod{pq},
\]
and choose its least nonnegative representative. Then
\[
0\le i<pq\le 150,
\]
so \(0\le i<150\), and the defining congruence gives
\[
a+id\equiv 0\pmod{pq}.
\]
Consequently both \(p\) and \(q\) divide \(a+id\). This term is positive because \(a\ge2\) and \(i,d\ge0\). It therefore has both \(p\) and \(q\) among its prime divisors. Their final digits are different, so the term is not lopsided. This proves the lemma.

It follows that if all 150 terms were lopsided, then for every pair of primes \(p,q\) with different final digits and \(pq\le150\), at least one of \(p,q\) would have to divide \(d\). We now show, by an exhaustive case analysis, that no \(d\le2025\) can satisfy this requirement.

We repeatedly use the following elementary fact. If several distinct primes all divide \(d\), then their product divides \(d\), since distinct primes are pairwise coprime. As \(d\ge1\), if an integer \(M\) divides \(d\), then \(M\le d\). Thus a product greater than 2025 cannot divide \(d\).

All the numbers used below as primes—namely
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17
\]
—are prime. In every displayed obstructing pair, the product is at most 150 and the two final digits are different.

We begin by splitting according to whether \(2\mid d\).

### Case 1: \(2\nmid d\)

Split according to whether \(3\mid d\).

* If \(3\nmid d\), use the pair \((2,3)\). Neither prime divides \(d\), their final digits are \(2\) and \(3\), and
  \[
  2\cdot3=6\le150.
  \]
  The obstruction lemma gives a non-lopsided term.

* Suppose \(3\mid d\). Split according to whether \(7\mid d\).

  * If \(7\nmid d\), use \((2,7)\): its final digits are \(2,7\), and \(2\cdot7=14\le150\).

  * Suppose \(7\mid d\). Split according to whether \(11\mid d\).

    * If \(11\nmid d\), use \((2,11)\): its final digits are \(2,1\), and \(2\cdot11=22\le150\).

    * Suppose \(11\mid d\). We claim that \(13\nmid d\). Otherwise \(3,7,11,13\) would all divide \(d\), so their product would divide \(d\). But
      \[
      3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=3003>2025,
      \]
      contradicting \(d\le2025\). Hence \(13\nmid d\). We may now use the pair \((2,13)\): neither divides \(d\), their final digits are \(2,3\), and
      \[
      2\cdot13=26\le150.
      \]

Thus every possibility with \(2\nmid d\) produces an obstructing pair.

### Case 2: \(2\mid d\)

We next split according to whether \(5\mid d\).

#### Case 2A: \(5\nmid d\)

Split according to whether \(3\mid d\).

* If \(3\nmid d\), use \((5,3)\). Their final digits are \(5,3\), and
  \[
  5\cdot3=15\le150.
  \]

* Suppose \(3\mid d\). Split according to whether \(7\mid d\).

  * If \(7\nmid d\), use \((5,7)\), whose product is \(35\le150\) and whose final digits are \(5,7\).

  * Suppose \(7\mid d\). Split according to whether \(11\mid d\).

    * If \(11\nmid d\), use \((5,11)\), whose product is \(55\le150\) and whose final digits are \(5,1\).

    * Suppose \(11\mid d\). Then \(13\nmid d\), because otherwise the distinct primes \(3,7,11,13\) would all divide \(d\), forcing
      \[
      3\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=3003
      \]
      to divide \(d\), which is impossible for \(d\le2025\). Thus neither \(5\) nor \(13\) divides \(d\). Use \((5,13)\): its final digits are \(5,3\), and
      \[
      5\cdot13=65\le150.
      \]

This deals with all possibilities in which \(2\mid d\) but \(5\nmid d\).

#### Case 2B: \(2\mid d\) and \(5\mid d\)

Split according to whether \(3\mid d\).

##### Case 2B(i): \(3\nmid d\)

Split according to whether \(7\mid d\).

* If \(7\nmid d\), use \((3,7)\). Their final digits are \(3,7\), and
  \[
  3\cdot7=21\le150.
  \]

* Suppose \(7\mid d\). Split according to whether \(11\mid d\).

  * If \(11\nmid d\), use \((3,11)\), whose final digits are \(3,1\) and whose product is \(33\le150\).

  * Suppose \(11\mid d\). We claim that \(17\nmid d\). Otherwise \(2,5,7,11,17\) would all divide \(d\), and hence
    \[
    2\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot17=13090
    \]
    would divide \(d\). This is impossible because \(13090>2025\ge d\). Therefore neither \(3\) nor \(17\) divides \(d\). Use \((3,17)\): its final digits are \(3,7\), and
    \[
    3\cdot17=51\le150.
    \]

This settles the subcase \(3\nmid d\).

##### Case 2B(ii): \(3\mid d\)

Thus at this point
\[
2\mid d,\qquad 3\mid d,\qquad 5\mid d.
\]
Split according to whether \(7\mid d\).

* First suppose \(7\nmid d\). Split according to whether \(11\mid d\).

  * If \(11\nmid d\), use \((7,11)\). Their final digits are \(7,1\), and
    \[
    7\cdot11=77\le150.
    \]

  * Suppose \(11\mid d\). Then \(13\nmid d\), since otherwise \(2,3,5,11,13\) would all divide \(d\), forcing
    \[
    2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11\cdot13=4290
    \]
    to divide \(d\), contrary to \(4290>2025\). Hence use \((7,13)\): neither prime divides \(d\), their final digits are \(7,3\), and
    \[
    7\cdot13=91\le150.
    \]

* It remains to suppose \(7\mid d\). We then have
  \[
  2\mid d,\quad3\mid d,\quad5\mid d,\quad7\mid d.
  \]
  We claim that neither \(11\) nor \(13\) divides \(d\). If \(11\mid d\), then
  \[
  2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310
  \]
  would divide \(d\), impossible because \(2310>2025\). Similarly, if \(13\mid d\), then
  \[
  2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13=2730
  \]
  would divide \(d\), again impossible. Therefore we can use the pair \((11,13)\). Its final digits are \(1,3\), and
  \[
  11\cdot13=143\le150.
  \]

This exhausts the case \(2\mid d\) and \(5\mid d\), and hence exhausts all possible positive integers \(d\le2025\).

In every terminal case we have found two primes \(p,q\), with different final decimal digits and with \(pq\le150\), such that neither divides \(d\). By the obstruction lemma, some term \(a+id\), with \(0\le i<150\), is divisible by both primes and is therefore not lopsided. This contradicts the assumption that all 150 terms are lopsided.

Consequently, there are no integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) for which every one of \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\), occurs in A381159. Thus the asserted arithmetic progression does not exist, disproving the conjecture.
